recent_posts.title: How I edit on one OS and run code on another (vagrant)
recent_posts.summary: A walkthrough of using Vagrant to create a headless Linux VM on a Mac, with a shared folder synced between the host and the VM. This lets you edit code natively in VS Code on macOS while compiling and running it inside Linux — no file copying needed. The setup involves a Vagrantfile (written in Ruby) that specifies the base Ubuntu image, provisioning packages, and a synced folder. Once the VM is up, you SSH in and any edits made on the Mac instantly appear inside the VM.

recent_posts.title: Const, const pointers, and pointers to const things (in C)
recent_posts.summary: The const keyword in C can be applied to variables and pointers in different ways. For simple variables, const can appear before or after the type ("west const" vs "east const"). With pointers, there are two distinct things you can make const: the pointer itself, or the data it points to. A "pointer to const int" means you can't change the value through dereferencing, but you can reassign the pointer. A "const pointer" means the pointer address can't change, but you can modify the pointed-to value. You can also combine both to create a const pointer to const data.

recent_posts.title: Thread local storage in C
recent_posts.summary: Thread-local storage in C allows variables to be scoped per thread rather than globally or locally to functions. Using the `thread_local` keyword (or variants like `__thread` or `_Thread_local`), each thread gets its own copy of a variable, preventing race conditions when multiple threads access shared state. This technique is demonstrated through a `strtok` implementation that uses static variables, showing how thread-local storage solves thread safety issues without major code refactoring. The approach is used in the C standard library for `errno` to maintain thread safety across traditional error handling patterns.

recent_posts.title: Understanding and fixing false sharing in multithreaded programs
recent_posts.summary: False sharing occurs when multiple threads access different variables that reside on the same CPU cache line, causing significant performance degradation. A simple example demonstrates how two separate counters being incremented by different threads can run 2x slower when adjacent in memory versus when separated. The issue stems from cache coherence protocols forcing cores to pass cache lines back and forth. Solutions include using memory alignment (alignas keyword in C) to ensure variables sit on separate 64-byte cache lines, trading minimal memory overhead for substantial performance gains in multi-threaded programs.

What is stream orientation? (fwide)
recent_posts.summary: Stream orientation in C determines whether a stream works with byte-oriented functions (like printf) or wide-character functions (like wprintf). Mixing these function types on the same stream causes undefined behavior. The fwide() function checks or sets a stream's orientation: negative values for byte-oriented, positive for wide-oriented, and zero to check without changing. Once set by the first I/O operation, orientation persists unless the stream is reopened with freopen(). Best practice is to choose one orientation and stick with it throughout your program.

recent_posts.title: What are wide characters?
recent_posts.summary: Wide characters (wchar_t) are a way to handle Unicode text in C/C++ programs using 4-byte integers that can store any Unicode code point. Unlike single-byte chars limited to ASCII, wide character arrays store text as UTF-32, making it simple to process strings character-by-character through direct indexing. The tutorial covers declaration syntax, printing with printf/wprintf, string functions like wcslen, and the need for locale configuration. While wide characters simplify processing logic, they consume 4x more memory than UTF-8 for ASCII-heavy text, making them better suited for internal processing than storage or network transmission.

recent_posts.title: A warning about the char type
recent_posts.summary: The char data type in C can cause portability issues because the C standard doesn't specify whether it's signed or unsigned—this is implementation-defined and varies across platforms. When a char holds values above 127, signed vs unsigned behavior differs significantly, especially with bitwise operations like right shifts. To write portable code, explicitly use 'unsigned char' or 'signed char', use fixed-width types like 'uint8_t' from stdint.h, or compile with the '-funsigned-char' flag to force unsigned behavior across all platforms.

recent_posts.title: What is Unicode?
recent_posts.summary: Unicode is a standardized numbering system that assigns unique numerical values to characters from all written languages and emojis, enabling computers worldwide to communicate without confusion. While ASCII used one byte per character (limiting to 256 symbols), Unicode supports thousands of characters through encoding schemes like UTF-8, which has become the default for the web. The tutorial demonstrates how different characters require varying byte lengths—English letters use one byte, while characters from languages like Khmer and emojis require multiple bytes.
